title: The True Cost of Returns for Indian D2C Brands
summary: Cost of COD returns in Indian D2C brands ₹561 per order on average — but working capital lockup, GST reconciliation, and lost customers cost even more. See what the numbers actually look like and how instant refunds change the equation.
body_markdown:
India’s D2C industry has a returns problem it hasn’t fully priced in yet.


Most founders track what’s visible. Reverse logistics. Restocking fees. Customer support tickets. But the real cost of a return runs much deeper than any line item on a P&L. It lives in the working capital locked in refund cycles, the customers who never come back after a slow experience, and the finance team hours spent reconciling what should have been automated a long time ago.


Here’s what the numbers actually look like.


**The Scale Nobody Talks About**


60% of Indian ecommerce is still COD. And 26% of those orders come back. That single combination changes the entire returns equation for D2C brands.


Fashion return rates in India sit between 25 and 35%. COD return-to-origin rates run between 20 and 40% of COD orders. For brands in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, where most new D2C growth is coming from, these numbers are even higher.


Each returned COD order costs a brand approximately Rs 561 on average, accounting for forward shipping, reverse shipping, blocked capital, and product damage. Multiply that by 26% of your COD volume, and the number gets uncomfortable fast.


But here’s what most articles stop at. The Rs 561 is what you can see. What you cannot see is often more expensive.


### **The Three Costs Nobody Is Tracking**


1. **Working capital locked in the refund window**


When a return is picked up, the refund clock starts for the customer. But the money does not move immediately. Between pickup confirmation, quality check, finance approval, and bank processing, the average COD refund takes 5 to 7 days to reach the customer.


During that window, the working capital is neither with the customer nor productively deployed by the brand. For a brand processing Rs 1 crore in COD returns every month, that is roughly Rs 16 to 23 lakhs sitting idle at any given point, earning nothing and doing nothing.


COD ties up cash for 5 to 10 extra days. If your 13-week cash flow is showing tight weeks, that locked capital is a real problem, not an accounting footnote.


[NewsGram](https://www.newsgram.com/business/2026/03/24/how-indian-e-commerce-companies-are-managing-the-returns-challenge)


1. **GST reconciliation chaos**


This one barely gets discussed. COD transactions create complex GST reconciliation issues. When remittances arrive in a different month than the dispatch, the tax treatment becomes complicated. Brands struggle to match GST outflows with actual cash inflows, especially when logistics partners do not provide GST-compliant remittance reports.


[forrester](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/13-06-10-indias_ecommerce_woes_managing_logistics_challenges_in_india)


For most mid-size D2C brands, this means a finance team spending hours every week on manual matching that should not exist. That is a real cost, even if it does not show up on a returns dashboard.


1. **The customer you lose without knowing it**


This is the most expensive cost and the hardest one to put on a spreadsheet.


Customers receiving instant refunds show a 23% higher repurchase rate in the following 30 days. The reverse is equally true. A slow or confusing refund experience is one of the top reasons customers do not come back.


In a category where customer acquisition costs keep rising, losing a customer at the refund stage is not just an operational miss. It is a revenue miss. The customer already bought from you. They were willing to return. The refund experience was the last impression your brand left on them.


### **Why COD Refunds Are Specifically Broken**


Prepaid refunds are straightforward. The money goes back to the card or UPI it came from. COD refunds are a different problem entirely.


The customer paid cash. You do not have their bank details. To send them money back, you need to collect their account number or UPI ID, verify it, and then process the transfer. Traditionally this means a customer support call, a form, a follow-up, and 5 to 7 days of waiting.


This is the structural reason COD refunds are slow. It is not a logistics problem. It is a money movement problem. And it is one that most logistics and operations articles completely miss because they are not looking at the finance layer.

**The Exchange Opportunity Nobody Is Fully Capturing**


Returns do not have to be refunds. An exchange is a better outcome for everyone. The brand keeps the revenue. The customer gets what they actually wanted. The relationship survives.


But most brands treat exchanges as an afterthought. The collection for the new order and the return of the old one happen in disconnected flows, with different teams managing each side.


Several D2C brands now offer instant exchange workflows where the replacement item ships before the original return is picked up. The impact on customer retention is substantial. But the money movement side of this, collecting payment for the new order while simultaneously processing the return credit, is rarely automated.


[Base](https://base.com/en-IN/blog/how-leading-indian-d2c-brands-use-oms-to-reduce-returns-and-speed-up-refunds/)


That gap is where significant revenue leaks out silently.


**What a 3-Minute Refund Is Actually Worth**


Here is a number worth sitting with. Customers receiving instant refunds show a 23% higher repurchase rate in the following 30 days.


For a brand with 1000 returning customers a month at an average order value of Rs 800, a 23% improvement in repurchase rate from that cohort alone is roughly Rs 1.84 lakhs in additional revenue every month. From refund speed. Not from marketing. Not from discounts.


The brands that have figured this out are not treating the refund as the end of a transaction. They are treating it as the beginning of the next one.


Wallet refunds make this even more powerful. When a customer gets their refund credited to a brand wallet instead of their bank account, the money stays in your ecosystem. Customers perceive wallet funds as store credit, something meant to be spent, not saved. That psychological shift drives faster repurchase.


**What the Best Brands Are Doing Differently**


The brands consistently outperforming on retention after returns share three things in common.


First, they have automated the trigger. The refund does not wait for a finance team approval. It fires the moment the return is confirmed at pickup.


Second, they give the customer a choice. Refund to source, refund to wallet, or exchange. Giving customers control over the outcome dramatically reduces friction and increases the likelihood of a second purchase.


Third, they have connected their logistics and finance layers. The ops team and the finance team are looking at the same data in real time. Brands that offer refund on pickup, where the money is released the moment the courier agent scans the item at the door, transform a negative experience into a positive one.


**The Way Forward**


Returns in Indian D2C are not going away. COD returns ran at 58% during the festive quarter. The question is not how to eliminate them. The question is how to make them cost less and retain more.

The brands that will win are the ones that stop treating returns as a cost to be minimised and start treating them as a customer moment to be designed. The refund experience is the last touchpoint before a customer decides whether to come back.


Right now, most brands are losing that moment by default. The infrastructure to win it already exists. It just needs to be connected.
